passage:
Coming back from my night shift at the packaging unit, I was stopped at the crossing by a police jeep. "Which basti are you from?" one officer asked, in a tone I have heard before. He turned my bag upside down and said if I answered back, he could "teach me a lesson". My hands were cold, but I kept my voice level. I noted his name, the time and the jeep's number, answered only what was asked, and phoned my brother, who said, "Stay where you are. I'm coming." They let me go once he arrived.
The next morning Mehak, a volunteer at a legal-aid clinic, helped me write everything on one page. We sent it to the senior officer. That same day a clerk gave us an acknowledgement number, and a call came to attend a hearing.
Sunaina

qa.a: Sunaina was coming back from a night shift at the packaging unit.

qa.q: What steps did Sunaina take that were safer than resisting?
qa.a: Sunaina noted the officer's name, the time and the jeep's number, answered only what was asked, phoned a brother, and sent a written complaint to the senior officer with Mehak's help.

qa.q: How did the senior officer's office respond to the written complaint?
qa.a: A clerk gave an acknowledgement number the same day, and a call came to attend a hearing.

passage:
Case note, written by Aparna.
Chandrika, twenty-four, works in a garment shop and lives in a resettlement colony. On Tuesday she went to the police station to report a stolen phone. The desk officer told her to wait outside and said people from her area "always exaggerate". She told me her face burned, but she did not argue. She noted the officer's badge number and the time, and rang her cousin, who came to sit with her.
She came to our clinic the next day. I helped her write a short, factual complaint. We sent it to the station's senior officer with a copy to a human-rights group, and I went with her. On Thursday the senior officer's office called her in, registered the theft and said the remark would be looked into.

qa.q: What did Chandrika go to the police station to report?
qa.a: Chandrika went to report a stolen phone.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when the desk officer said people from her area always exaggerate?
qa.a: Chandrika felt humiliated and angry, since her face burned, but she stayed calm and did not argue.

qa.q: What steps did Chandrika take that protected her?
qa.a: Chandrika noted the badge number and the time, called her cousin, and then wrote a factual complaint with Aparna's help that went to the senior officer and a human-rights group.

qa.q: Why might Aparna go with Chandrika instead of filing on her behalf?
qa.a: Aparna probably wanted Chandrika to lead her own complaint while having support beside her, which the note suggests by saying Aparna went with her.

grounding: A young person from a low-income colony feels talked down to at a police station, and recording facts and involving family and a legal-aid worker is safer than resisting.

passage:
Thursday night
Still shaking. At the checkpoint near our basti tonight, the constable looked at my ID, saw my surname and address, and his whole tone changed. "Where are you coming from at this hour? People from there are always up to something." He kept me standing for twenty minutes while he let others go.
I wanted to shout and cry. I did neither. I said, calmly, "Sir, I'm coming from work. Here's my office ID." I noted his name tag and the time in my head.
Afterwards I called Akash Bhaiya and told him everything. He said, "Write it down tonight, every word."
So I have. Tomorrow Akash and I will go to the legal aid clinic, where a rights-group volunteer sits on Fridays.
I'm tired of being made to feel small. But I'm not going to be quiet about it.
Ankita

qa.q: How long did the constable keep Ankita standing?
qa.a: He kept Ankita standing for twenty minutes while he let others go.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when the constable's tone changed?
qa.a: Ankita felt humiliated and angry, wanting to shout and cry, and made to feel small because of the surname and address.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that was safer than resisting?
qa.a: Ankita stayed calm, noted the officer's name and the time, wrote everything down, told Akash Bhaiya and planned to go to the legal aid clinic with a rights volunteer.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when he hears what happened?
qa.a: Akash probably feels angry and protective, which is why he tells Ankita to write every word down.

grounding: A young adult from a poor neighbourhood is talked down to at a checkpoint, and stays calm, records the facts and involves family and legal aid.

passage:
In their kasba near Gaya, Rashmi, twenty-five, went to the police outpost with her brother Kunal to report that a neighbour had moved the boundary stones of their small field. The head constable barely looked up. "Your kind always makes land trouble. Go home, or I'll register a case against you instead."
Kunal's fists clenched. Rashmi put a hand on his arm. "Not here," she whispered.
She said, calmly, "Sir, we only want our complaint recorded." When he refused again, she thanked him politely and left.
Outside, Kunal was furious. "Why didn't you fight him?"
"Because that's what he wanted," Rashmi said. She wrote down the date, time and his words on the back of a bill.
That week, she went to the district legal aid office and a Dalit rights group in the town. With their help, she sent a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police. A week later, an officer came to measure the field.

qa.q: What had the neighbour done?
qa.a: The neighbour had moved the boundary stones of their small field.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she put a hand on Kunal's arm?
qa.a: Rashmi felt tense and afraid that things would get worse, but determined to stay calm and not give the constable an excuse.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi's approach safer and more effective?
qa.a: She stayed calm, recorded the facts, and went to legal aid and a rights group to send a written complaint, which led to action without risking a fight.

qa.q: How might Kunal see his sister after the officer came?
qa.a: Kunal would likely feel proud and relieved, seeing that her calm approach worked better than fighting.

grounding: In a small town, a young woman from a lower-caste family is threatened by a constable, and records facts and involves legal aid and a rights group instead of resisting.

passage: Outside the train station in Lyon, two officers stopped Camila for the third time that month. She was on her way to her shift at the laundry, in her work tunic. One of them held her residence card up to the light and said loudly, "People like you always have fake papers." A passenger slowed down to stare. Camila's stomach turned to ice. She wanted to snatch the card back. Instead she kept her hands still and visible and her voice low. "The card is real. May I have your badge numbers, please?" They gave them, annoyed, and let her go. At the laundry she wrote everything down on the back of a receipt: the time, the place, the words, the numbers. That evening her cousin Esther took her to a rights association near the market, where a volunteer lawyer helped her file a formal complaint.

qa.q: Where was Camila going when she was stopped?
qa.a: She was on her way to her shift at the laundry.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling when the officer said her papers were fake?
qa.a: Camila felt frightened and humiliated, her stomach turning to ice, and angry enough to want to snatch the card back.

qa.q: Which of Camila's choices kept her safer?
qa.a: Keeping her hands visible and voice low, asking for badge numbers, writing down the facts, and going with Esther to a rights association.

qa.q: How might Esther see what happened to Camila?
qa.a: Esther seems to see it as unfair treatment worth challenging, which is why she took Camila to a rights association that same evening.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman from a minority background talked down to by officers who stays calm, records the facts and involves family and a rights group instead of resisting.
